challenges.title: Binary Search
challenges.prompt:
Given an array of distinct integers `nums` sorted in ascending order and a `target`, return the index of `target` in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not there.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: Values are distinct and sorted ascending
hints: Keep the invariant: if the target is present, it lies in nums[lo..hi].
Loop while lo <= hi. Compare nums[mid] with the target and move lo to mid + 1 or hi to mid - 1.
Compute mid as lo + (hi - lo) // 2 (or Math.floor in JavaScript) so it is a whole number.
challenges.explanation: The inclusive template keeps the target, if present, inside nums[lo..hi]. Each comparison discards mid and one half, so the range shrinks every step; when it is empty, the target is absent.

challenges.title: Search Insert Position
challenges.prompt:
Given a sorted array of distinct integers `nums` and a `target`, return the index of `target` if it is present. Otherwise return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: Values are distinct and sorted ascending
hints: You want the first index whose value is at least the target: the lower bound.
Use a half-open range with lo = 0 and hi = len(nums), because the answer can be past the end.
While lo < hi: if nums[mid] < target, lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid. Return lo.
challenges.explanation: This is the lower bound: everything before lo is smaller than the target and everything from hi on is at least the target. When they meet, lo is both the target's index (if present) and its insert position. Starting hi at len(nums) allows the after-the-end answer.

challenges.title: Minimum of a Rotated Sorted Array
challenges.prompt:
An array of distinct integers was sorted in ascending order and then rotated some number of times (possibly zero), so `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` might have become `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`.

Given the rotated array `nums`, return its smallest element in O(log n) time.

examples.explain: The sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] was rotated 3 times.

hints: The array is two sorted runs; the minimum is where the second run starts.
Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If nums[mid] is bigger, the drop is to the right of mid.
Otherwise mid..hi is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left: hi = mid. Loop while lo < hi.
challenges.explanation: If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the rotation point lies in (mid, hi]; otherwise mid..hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or before it. This is the first-true template, so hi = mid pairs with a mid that rounds down. Comparing with nums[hi] also handles an unrotated array.

challenges.title: Search in a Rotated Sorted Array
challenges.pattern: Binary search on the sorted half
challenges.prompt:
An array of distinct integers was sorted in ascending order and then rotated at an unknown point, for example `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`. Given the rotated array `nums` and a `target`, return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it is not present.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
hints: Around any mid, at least one half (lo..mid or mid..hi) is sorted.
If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted; otherwise the right half is.
If the target lies within the sorted half's range, search that half; otherwise search the other one.
challenges.explanation: Use the inclusive template. At each mid one half is sorted, found by comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid] (<= so a one-element left half counts as sorted). A sorted half has a known range, so you can tell whether the target is inside it and discard the other half.

challenges.title: Minimum Printing Speed
challenges.prompt:
A print shop has print jobs, where `jobs[i]` is the number of pages in job `i`, and `hours` hours to finish all of them. The printer runs at an integer speed of `s` pages per hour. Each hour it works on one job only: it prints up to `s` pages of that job, and if the job had fewer than `s` pages left, it finishes the job and stays idle for the rest of that hour.

Return the minimum speed `s` that finishes every job within `hours` hours. There are always at least as many hours as jobs.

examples.explain: At speed 4: 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours. At speed 3 it takes 10.
With one hour per job, the speed must cover the largest job.

hints: If speed s finishes in time, so does every faster speed. The answers form no, ..., no, yes, ..., yes.
Search speeds from 1 to max(jobs). For a speed s, the hours needed are the sum of ceil(pages / s).
Find the first feasible speed: if mid works, hi = mid; otherwise lo = mid + 1. Use integer ceiling division.
challenges.explanation: Feasibility is monotonic in the speed, so binary search the speeds 1 to max(jobs) for the first one that fits. Each check sums integer ceilings over the jobs. max(jobs) always works because there is at least one hour per job.

complexity.time: O(n log M), where M is the largest job

challenges.title: Search a Sorted Grid
challenges.pattern: Binary search on a flattened index
challenges.prompt:
Each row of the grid `matrix` is sorted in increasing order, and the first value of every row is greater than the last value of the row above it, so reading the rows one after another gives a single sorted list. Return `true` if `target` is in the grid.

Aim for O(log(rows * cols)).

examples.explain: 21 would sit between 20 and 25, at the boundary between two rows.

hints: Treat the grid as one sorted list of length rows * cols without copying it.
Position i of that imaginary list is the cell at row `i // cols`, column `i % cols`.
Run an ordinary binary search on `lo = 0`, `hi = rows * cols - 1`, reading values through that formula.
challenges.explanation: Because each row starts above where the previous one ended, the grid is one sorted list folded into rows. Mapping a flat index i to (i // cols, i % cols) lets a standard inclusive binary search run over it directly, in O(log(rows * cols)) with no copying. Two binary searches (first pick the row, then search inside it) are equally fast and also fine to present.
